paras: The Waterloo attack on emigration agent John Milam took place on the evening of July 20, 1885, when white residents of Waterloo, Laurens County, South Carolina, drove off a railway agent who had come to take six Black women to Arkansas. Milam's own account, carried by an Atlanta wire, said a mob shot at him, tied and beat him, while Waterloo residents said he was only warned and fled after shots fired in the air. Black newspapers presented the case as proof that white Southerners would use force to keep Black laborers from leaving.

Milam was a passenger or emigration agent of the East Tennessee, Virginia & Georgia Railway, and Waterloo was a new town on the Greenwood, Laurens and Spartanburg Railroad. According to the local investigation, planters had heard that Black laborers meant to leave on August 1, and having advanced supplies to them under labor contracts, they feared for their crops. Milam said he had come to carry six women to their husbands in Arkansas, but residents suspected he meant to entice contract laborers away.

In the Atlanta wire version, one of the women told Milam that the white people had threatened to kill the first Negro who tried to leave, and the depot agent warned him to go. Three men then called the hotel proprietor into the yard, after which the proprietor showed Milam out a back gate toward a swamp and gave a yell that brought a mob after him. The wire said about twenty shots were fired at him amid cries of "kill him," and that the mob tied his hands, beat him and made him walk four hours beside their horses before leaving him with a threat of death if he returned. He fainted in the woods, was picked up by a farmer and taken to a station, and reached Atlanta in a serious condition.

A variant printed in Honolulu added that a man named Casper Smith collected a mob of sixty and that the men kicked and cuffed Milam before leaving him. The Cleveland Gazette's shorter version said the mob carried him from his hotel and whipped him "most brutally."

The News and Courier sent a correspondent to Laurens County to look into several recent outrages, and he relied on statements that Laurensville Herald editor F. B. Crews had gathered from the hotel proprietor H. C. Fuller, Casper Smith, W. F. Cobb and other residents. Farmers at the depot told him they had used no violence and hoped Milam's story would spread and keep emigration agents away. No report of arrests or any legal proceeding against the Waterloo men appears in the coverage.

The Cleveland Gazette ran the story on August 1 in its column of news about "our people," closing with the remark that Southern whites valued Black people only for their labor. On August 8 the New York Freeman printed the full Atlanta dispatch under the headline "RUFFIAN BRUTALITY. The Mob Prevents Colored People from Leaving." Below it the Freeman printed an unattributed quoted passage urging Black Southerners to arm and to kill anyone who killed a man for trying to take his family away, observing that "the right to run away" was the only right left them.

White papers far from South Carolina, in Kansas, West Virginia and Hawaii, reprinted the wire as news, the Honolulu Daily Bulletin under the heading "MOB RULE IN THE SOUTH." South Carolina papers answered differently: the Savannah Morning News's state column reported that the "Gentlemen of Waterloo" called the story untrue, and the News and Courier judged it "greatly exaggerated." Even so, the News and Courier conceded that the "pistol salute" suggested Milam had not left too soon and called it significant that emigration agents had to be banished "at the point of the pistol."

The beating story came from Milam himself, as told to the Atlanta Journal, while the denial came from the Waterloo residents who had confronted him. The News and Courier's correspondent accepted the residents' version that one man fired three or four shots in the air and that Milam "was not touched or bullied," but neither account comes from an independent witness.

bases: Every account agrees that Waterloo residents gathered against Milam, warned him off and fired shots as he left to stop him taking Black laborers away (A3, A4, A6); whether he was also beaten is contested (A2, A4), and no organized band is named.

The Atlanta wire, from Milam's own account, says he was shot at, tied and beaten (A2, A6, A7), while Waterloo residents and the News and Courier's investigator say he was only warned and fled after shots in the air (A3, A4, A5).

accounts.gist: Warned that whites would kill the first person to help Negroes leave, Milam was sent out the hotel's back gate, pursued by a mob firing about twenty shots, tied, beaten and marched four hours through the woods before a farmer found him.

accounts.label: Waterloo residents and News and Courier investigator
accounts.gist: Milam talked secretly with contract laborers, a group of farmers gathered, he was told to satisfy them or leave, and one man fired pistol shots in the air as he went; he was not touched.
